Doppler pass

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how a pass’s range-rate history changes with distance from the ground track.

In the straight constant-speed pass model, slant range is r(t) = √[h² + b² + (vt)²], with height h, cross-track distance b, and t = 0 at closest approach.

Range rate is v²t/r(t), so first-order Doppler is −(fc/c)v²t/r(t). The zero crossing occurs at closest approach, and its slope magnitude is fc v²/[c√(h² + b²)].

A more distant track gives a gentler zero-crossing slope. Because this model contains b², the two sides of the ground track produce the same ideal history; additional information resolves that ambiguity.

Example

Changing cross-track distance from b = 0 to b = h increases closest slant range by √2. The zero-crossing slope magnitude falls to 1/√2 of its original value.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Can this ideal single-pass Doppler curve distinguish a beacon at cross-track distance +b from one at −b? Explain.

    Inspect how b enters both range and range rate.

    The curves are identical because b enters as b². A second pass, another measurement type, or additional position knowledge is needed to distinguish the two sides.
